rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The piece's main claim is that most published research findings in biomedical science are false — not just occasionally wrong, but false more often than not, as a matter of statistical structure rather than isolated error [spya-xpu5tw]. The abstract states this plainly: "There is increasing concern that most current published research findings are false.", and sets out that this probability depends on study power, bias, the number of competing studies, and the ratio of true to false relationships being tested in a field [spya-rupg9e].

The argument proper runs through the body of the piece in three stages:

1. A mathematical model, where Ioannidis derives the "positive predictive value" (the chance a statistically significant finding is actually true) from pre-study odds, statistical power, and significance level, showing a finding is more likely true than false only under certain conditions [spya-hjja9x].
2. Two refinements to that model — bias [spya-j7femp spya-s46ctb] and the effect of many independent teams testing the same question [spya-zjre9m spya-u5x4p2] — both of which push the probability of truth down further.
3. A worked example and six corollaries drawn from the model, covering study size, effect size, number of tested relationships, design flexibility, conflicts of interest, and "hot" competitive fields, each explaining a condition under which findings are less likely to be true [spya-c5mfye spya-vzv8aq spya-p2upz7 spya-f65pfg spya-hkh8ey spya-s4b0q7 spya-mgrr58].

The piece then generalizes this into simulations showing most designs and fields fall below 50% reliability [spya-j5xgg2 spya-umhdpk], and closes with proposed fixes: bigger, better-powered studies, registration of studies, and more honest accounting of pre-study odds [spya-t4k903 spya-a2jbw9 spya-fa6b0w spya-mjwvkp].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “Corollary 1: The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific” mean?
rows.text:
This paragraph says that findings from small studies are less likely to be true than findings from large studies [spya-vzv8aq]. The reason given is about statistical power — a study's ability to detect a real effect if one exists: smaller sample sizes mean lower power, and lower power pulls the probability that a "significant" result is actually true down toward the point where it's a coin flip (what the article calls 1 − β = 0.05) [spya-vzv8aq].

It then gives two contrasting examples from the article itself: fields that typically run large studies, like randomized controlled trials in heart disease research involving several thousand people, tend to produce more trustworthy findings than fields that typically run small studies, like research looking for molecular predictors of disease, where the article notes sample sizes can be 100 times smaller [spya-vzv8aq].

My inference is that this is the first of several corollaries building on the mathematical framework laid out earlier in the piece — each one isolates a single factor (here, study size) and states how it alone affects the odds that a published finding is genuinely true, holding everything else constant.

rows.question: Which paragraph gives the strongest support for the central claim, going only on the piece itself?
rows.text:
My inference is that the paragraph carrying the most weight is the one presenting the simulation results across study types, which turns the abstract algebra into concrete numbers: it reports that even a well-conducted, adequately powered randomized trial starting from 50-50 odds comes out true only about 85% of the time, while early-phase trials, exploratory epidemiology, and discovery-oriented genomics research fall far lower, often to a tiny fraction [spya-umhdpk].

The earlier derivation of the PPV formula [spya-hjja9x] and the bias/multi-team extensions [spya-s46ctb spya-u5x4p2] are what make this result possible, but they are the machinery; the paragraph at [spya-umhdpk] is where that machinery is run against realistic field-by-field parameters and shown, case by case, to push the probability of truth below 50% almost everywhere — which is the actual content of the title's claim.

rows.question: What does the author mean by positive predictive value?
rows.text: The author uses "positive predictive value" (PPV) to mean the probability that a research finding claimed as statistically significant is actually true, once the study has been run — in other words, the share of "positive" (significant) results that correspond to real relationships rather than false ones [spya-hjja9x]. He introduces it while setting up a 2×2 table comparing research claims against the real, "gold standard" relationships in a field, and defines it as the complement of what another paper called the false positive report probability [spya-hjja9x]. He then gives the formula PPV = (1 − β)R/(R − βR + α), where R is the pre-study ratio of true to false relationships being tested, β is the Type II error rate (related to study power), and α is the significance threshold (commonly 0.05) [spya-hjja9x]. The rest of the essay tracks how this PPV is driven down further once bias and competing research teams are factored in [spya-j7femp spya-zjre9m].

rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The main claim is that most published research findings are false — stated directly in the title and opening: there is concern that false findings may be the majority of published claims, and that this "can be proven" [spya-xpu5tw].

The argument is built in two stages:

1. A probability model (the "Modeling the Framework for False Positive Findings" section) shows that whether a finding is true depends on study power, the significance threshold, and — crucially — the pre-study odds that a true relationship exists at all in that field. From a 2×2 table of true/false relationships, the piece derives the positive predictive value (PPV) of a claimed finding, showing a finding is more likely true than false only under certain conditions on power and prior odds [spya-hjja9x]. It then extends the model to include bias (design, analysis, and reporting distortions that manufacture false "findings") and to the effect of many independent teams testing the same question, both of which drive the PPV down further [spya-gfvava spya-j7femp spya-zjre9m].

2. From that model, six corollaries are drawn — small studies, small effect sizes, many/unselected tested relationships, flexible designs, conflicts of interest, and "hot" competitive fields all lower the chance that a given finding is true [spya-nx5jjr spya-vzv8aq spya-p2upz7 spya-f65pfg spya-hkh8ey spya-s4b0q7 spya-mgrr58]. Simulations then show that under realistic combinations of these factors, PPV exceeding 50% is hard to achieve across most study designs and fields [spya-j5xgg2 spya-umhdpk].

rows.question: What does the final paragraph of the article say?
rows.text:
The final paragraph argues that most new discoveries will keep coming from hypothesis-generating research with low or very low pre-study odds of being true, so a single study's statistical significance only gives a partial picture — it tells you nothing about how much testing went on elsewhere in the field. It adds that even with the large statistical literature on correcting for multiple testing, it's usually impossible to know how much data dredging by the authors or other teams preceded a reported finding, and even knowing that wouldn't tell you the pre-study odds. The conclusion is that researchers must make subjective, approximate assumptions about how many tested relationships in a field are likely to be true, drawing on the wider field and on biases seen in neighboring fields — and that despite being subjective, these assumptions are still useful for interpreting and contextualizing research claims [spya-y44q7p].

rows.question: What does the final paragraph of the article say?
rows.text:
The final paragraph argues that even with better methods, most new discoveries will keep coming from hypothesis-generating research where the odds a tested relationship is true are low or very low, so a single study's statistical significance only gives a partial picture without knowing how much other testing has gone on in the field. It adds that even though multiple-testing corrections exist in the statistical literature, it is usually impossible to know how much data dredging preceded a finding, and that knowing this wouldn't tell us the pre-study odds anyway. So Ioannidis concludes researchers must make subjective, approximate assumptions about how many tested relationships are likely true in a given field and research design, drawing on the wider field and on biases seen in neighboring fields — and that despite being subjective, such assumptions are still useful for interpreting and contextualizing research claims [spya-y44q7p].

rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The main claim is that if you want to think clearly, you should let as few things become part of your identity as possible, since people can't reason well about anything tied to who they think they are [spya-xv45wq].

The argument builds in steps: it opens by asking why religion and politics produce uselessly circular arguments, and suggests it's because anyone can have an opinion on them without needing expertise [spya-pfruy3 spya-dpvyy2]. It then rejects the idea that this happens because these topics have no definite answers, noting that even precise political questions suffer the same fate [spya-gv44uj]. The real cause, the piece argues, is that religion and politics become part of people's identity, and people become partisan — unable to argue fruitfully — about anything bound up with who they are [spya-kwzcxp]. A supporting example shows this isn't really about the topic but about identification: debates over old Bronze Age battles don't turn political the way modern ones do, because no one identifies with a side in them [spya-uz3ta2]. The programming-languages example extends this, showing that even a topic that often becomes a "religious war" can still have a real, better-or-worse answer, so long as the people discussing it aren't arguing from identity [spya-s6tp4k]. From there the piece draws its general rule — fruitful discussion is possible only where identity isn't engaged [spya-zdmhnz] — and lands on the conclusion already noted: keep your identity as small as possible, ideally not even labeling yourself as a believer in some view, since "the more labels you have for yourself, the dumber they make you" [spya-nt9xpg].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “More generally, you can have a fruitful discussion about a” mean?
rows.text:
That paragraph generalizes the point just made about programming-language debates: a topic is safe to discuss productively only insofar as nobody arguing about it has tied their sense of self to one side of it [spya-zdmhnz]. Politics and religion are especially bad because they pull in almost everyone's identity, but the same mechanism can make even a trivial-seeming topic unsafe — Paul Graham's example is arguing about Ford versus Chevy pickup trucks with people who've made that brand loyalty part of who they are [spya-zdmhnz]. So the same subject can be either fine or a minefield depending on who's in the room, not on anything inherent to the subject itself.

My inference is that this paragraph is the pivot of the essay: it moves the claim from "religion and politics are special" to "identity is the actual variable," which sets up the final move — that the fix isn't picking safer topics but keeping your own identity small [spya-xv45wq].
